# Neo4j

Native property-graph database. Nodes carry labels and properties, relationships are first-class,
typed, directed and can carry properties of their own — which is the feature the one project using it
here depends on.

## Where it is used

Lab 6 of [[discrete-mathematics-laboratories]], run on **Neo4j Desktop** with a local database and
the Desktop import folder. The model is a bipartite
`(:Object)-[:HAS_VALUE {value}]->(:Attribute)` graph representing a
[[pawlak-information-system]] — the attribute value lives on the *relationship*, which is precisely
what a relational table cannot express without a join table.

**It genuinely ran.** Confirmed in interview:

- 39 `:Object` nodes, 25 `:Attribute` nodes, **975 `HAS_VALUE` relationships** — real counts from a
  live instance, `confidence: high`.
- Uniqueness constraints on node keys, which also give index-backed `MERGE` — see
  [[idempotent-loading]].
- An optional `Object → Group(grade) → Group(class)` hierarchy (14 grades, 2 classes) layered over
  the base graph.
- Q0–Q6 report queries reading the structure back out.

The Desktop workflow itself is the deliverable's other half: `guide.txt` walks database creation, the
import-folder location, opening the Query pane, and the schema visualisation. The GUI import tool is
explicitly rejected in favour of scripts — [[cypher-scripts-over-neo4j-import-tool]].

## Compared with

The relational alternative for the same data is a wide 39×25 table; the graph form makes "which
objects share this attribute value" a traversal rather than a self-join. Contrast with the star
schema treatment of the same kind of question in
[[data-warehousing-and-business-intelligence]], and with the RDF/triple-store framing in
[[information-systems-modelling]].
